newsitem.title: UK: West's silence on Chechnya vote shows deep unease.
newsitem.headline: West's silence on Chechnya vote shows deep unease.

text.p: The West is maintaining a discreet silence on Chechnya's elections, anxious to avoid further upsetting Moscow at a crucial time for NATO's enlargement plans and adding to the pressures on Russian President Boris Yeltsin.

Diplomats say the United States and its European allies are keen not to offend Russian sensibilities before Monday's presidential polls in the breakaway Caucasus region, which will endorse eventual independence from Moscow whoever wins.

Too much is at stake as NATO tries to strike a deal with a deeply suspicious Russia over its plans to take in new members from Eastern Europe, if possible before a summit in July at which the alliance will invite the first countries to join.
"We are playing for stakes this year that are much higher than Chechnya, so you won't find anyone having much to say about the elections," said one diplomat.

The West believes that Yeltsin still represents the best hope for stable change in Russia but also knows that the president, still frail after heart surgery, is fighting off opponents who charge that he is unfit to rule.
"Adding to Yeltsin's problems by playing into the hands of hardliners and seeming to interfere in internal Russian affairs would be very unwise," said another envoy.

Russia insists that Chechnya remains part of the federation and the extreme sensitivity on this issue was underlined recently, when members of the Russian parliament criticised the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) for its role in helping organise next week's elections.
But the West is also keeping a low profile because it is troubled by the implications of Monday's vote, which touch on arguments over what exactly consitutes a country or nation.

The end of the Cold War brought many changes in Europe's borders. Some, like the dissolution of Czechoslovakia into two republics or the end of the Soviet Union, were largely peaceful. Others were not, as the collapse of Yugoslavia showed.

During almost two years of appalling bloodshed in Chechnya, Western countries were horrified by the killing but accepted Russia's argument that Chechnya was a part of its territory and had to remain so.
Kremlin fears that Chechen independence could tempt other regions to do the same and lead to the break-up the Russian Federation were shared to some extent in Western capitals.

Moscow and Chechen separatist leaders agreed to elections for a regional president and parliament under a peace accord signed last August, but agreed to leave aside the question of Chechnya's status for five years to let passions settle.

If Chechen leaders decide, with a popular mandate behind them, to renew the pressure for independence, the West may have to deal with the threat of renewed bloodshed and some difficult moral questions.
"We will have to ask ourselves whether it is right to deny people the right to independence if that is what they voted for," said one Western envoy.
So far, there is no sign that Western countries will change their position and risk a major row with Moscow.
But if they do not, they may be open to charges of hypocrisy since European countries and the United States recognised Bosnia and Croatia when they broke away from Yugoslavia.

"We know that the question of whether Chechnya will be independent has to be dealt with sooner or later and next week's elections will bring that closer," said one diplomat. "For now, it's not something that we need to get involved in."
